en: Past the swelling mountain ridge,
In haze beyond the reach of sight,
From the nose of the gray hill
An immense cloud of dust surged up.
His ribs trembling,
Wondering what strange disaster this might be,
Brave Kogoi stood and said,
Beginning these words to Ebegei:
“Ebegei, my twin,
My equal, a pillar of the world,
My companion in dust when we scout,
My companion through life,
My sheltered vale rich in livestock,
My keen-bladed steel
That splits a rock into forty pieces—
Did you see what I saw?
Did you sense what I sensed?
The drifting dust divides;
It seems an envoy is approaching,
A mediator among the people.
If he is a brave man and an envoy,
Let us make him a sworn friend
And draw out his secret.
If he is an enemy, a foe,
Let us lie down with his head for a pillow.
Let us not reveal the lower road,
Nor let the Kyrgyz, blessed by Kydyr,
Yield even a sliver of their secret.
Let us face his wind head-on
And learn how much cunning he has.”
So the two lions,
Grinding their teeth, unable to stay still,
Girded themselves, trusting in fate,
And stood watching carefully.
Riding a strangely fashioned mount,
The coarse tail of the mule beneath him
Knotted with a sharp twist,
Facing dust with dust,
Gauging their strength and watching their actions,
Zhelzhetpes came bearing news.
Speaking quietly but with weight,
He began a long and matchless speech;
Whoever heard it gave full attention,
For every precious word he spoke
Loomed like a towering mountain:
“Ebegei and Kogoi, two lions,
We are scouts who have come before you,
Envoys come to voice our grief,
Confidants who disclose secrets,
Men who have watched you from afar.
We have seen much slaughter by khans
And, heroes, have wandered without refuge.
When I lived in Kakan,
Among the forty khans of the Black Chinese,
I was no commoner, but a khan;
No open field, but a city;
No hollow, but a fortress;
No weakling, but a mighty man.
I was one of the sons who wore
A pearl-studded plume and coral stones,
One of the sons who understood
The Chinese affairs of judgment,
One of the heroes who rode the clouds,
Scattering frost as he went.
My ancestor four generations back was true Kyrgyz;
When his mother was six months pregnant,
The Chinese captured her as spoil.
With no blessing to make him a father,
With no marriage rite to make her a mother,
She was a palace maiden before the khan.
Among the palace maidens,
In the imperial garden,
In the city of Bakburchun,
My mother bore my forefather.
My forefather became a Kaldai khan;
My earlier ancestor passed away.
Thus four generations of my fathers
Lived among the Chinese as Kaldais,
And the fourth ancestor departed.
When I reached seven years of age,
My mother and father died.
I was raised by the treasury;
The diviners approved me,
Saying I would become lord of Beijing.
No living thing could match my racer.
A tribe called Kunde
Served its khan;
They were charged with raising me.
I was allotted the finest racer;
Because no wind could catch me when I galloped,
Because I proved consummately swift,
They named me Zhelzhetpes—‘Wind-Cannot-Catch.’
But lately in Chinese Kakan,
One mouth appeared beneath another,
One tongue beneath another;
Slander closed in upon my head,
My life was pressed so hard,
My strength was exhausted and spent,
And every means I had was gone.
Beaten with a cudgel by Chynteñir,
Finding neither protector nor refuge,
Heroes, I fled here in desperation
With eleven brave companions.
We are exiles, sundered from our people;
My two uncles, Ebegei and Kogoi,
We have fallen into your hands.”
When the two lions, Ebegei and Kogoi,
Heard this news,
They raised a gold-crescent banner,
And sent an uproar through the many Kyrgyz:
“God has sent us a lion!”
They pledged a horse for the ai-tuyak sacrifice
And swiftly pledged possessions of every kind.
To Kenen, rider of Kertulpar,
That lion-like champion
Who commanded the moonlit world,
They sent six fleet horses
And a letter written by Ebegei,
Bearing news to their khan
And now to all the many Kyrgyz
Whose ears could hear and eyes could see.
In the fruitful gardens of Talas,
Upon brave Kenen’s throne,
There was neither sorrow nor care.
Not even in his deepest dreams
Did he imagine the vast Chinese host would come;
There was no sign, no deed to suggest
That a furious enemy would engulf them.
The heroic steeds grazed on summer pasture,
The milking mares stood tethered;
Boots off and legs outstretched,
Kicking up their heels and tossing their caps,
The multitude lay resting.
While the people rested at ease,
Word and letter reached
The lion, brave Kenen;
Trouble swiftly struck, as you can see—
It was the letter of Ebegei and Kogoi.
The letter said Chynteñir had left Beijing
And was coming across
The rugged ridges of the Ala-Too,
Marching in to trample the world
As though it were ash.
His forty tribes had risen,
An army equal to an age;
They came inflicting boundless torment,
It said, advancing in full force.
They came well prepared
With disorder, strife, and calamity;
They came overwhelming all before them,
Taking many lands they encountered;
They came trampling everything flat,
Making hills and hollows level ground.
The letter was accurate and clear.
It was time to tell
The small white-capped people
Of the mad Teñir’s campaign.
It was time to set the people on one path
And, rather than remain alive,
Depart from this world.
When he heard this news,
Could brave Kenen remain still?
Would he let his people be overrun,
Or would God strike Kenen down?
Startling the heroes,
He saddled Kertulpar,
Who never faltered when mounted for battle.
He put on his armored coat,
With collar of gold and sleeves of bronze,
Its sharp mail proof against arrows,
And pulled a deep-blue iron helmet
Down over his head.
Without casting lots he now knew
How fierce the enemy was.
He made all his gear ready,
A gleaming sword and iron-headed mace,
A matchlock and a battle-axe—
He girded on all his weapons.
He covered peerless Kertulpar,
His prancing dark bay,
With an arrow-proof caparison.
Wearing an arrow-proof coat,
Mounted on a steed no arrow could catch,
He received blessings from the renowned,
And rode out against the furious foe,
Hardened like a black lion;
His wrath rose at the looming hardship.
For the white-capped Kyrgyz people,
For the soaring Ala-Too,
For our sage and for honor,
The dear lion staked
His precious life upon a hair.
Tempered like a keen sword,
Hardened like finest steel,
His lion’s aspect showing,
He departed from the Ala-Too.
Receiving leave and directions from the heroes,
He took a great host from the Kyrgyz.
Do not ask how large that host was:
He clad them in arrow-proof armor,
Mounted them on fiery steeds,
And had those who knew the route lead.
To scout the broad, open mountains,
To lend their strength
To the wolves Ebegei and Kogoi,
Kenen rode out without delay.
He traveled along the back
Of the ancestral Ala-Too,
For many days and many nights,
The eagle traveling without tiring;
He shot deer on the rough ground,
Argali upon the hills,
Ibex from the terraces,
And wild asses in the broken country.
Beyond the Bel-Moinok pass,
On the far side toward Urumchi,
At broad Shyikoo by Maral-Bashy,
On the far side of Tal-Mazar,
In the plain of the city of Urum,
Upon the ridge by the famed city
Of your renowned father Manas,
The massed army had its leader,
With giant Kenen at its head.
All the heroes were eager;
Your two uncles, Ebegei and Kogoi,
Met the hero Zhelzhetpes.
They spread the whole army across the ground,
Boiled a fat, mare-fed colt
To provide them food;
Fires burned for every group of ten,
The troops divided by tens,
A great communal cauldron in their midst,
Its rich broth spilling over.
The horses were tethered in a hollow,
On bear-skin pads and white felt
The champions’ horses could be seen,
While the army lay resting.
The two lions, Ebegei and Kogoi,
Stood beside brave Kenen.
Speaking quietly but with weight,
Ebegei and Kogoi began:
“Hero Kenen, you are an eagle;
You will do all that you know how to do.
You will stand beneath the banner,
Yet matters have suddenly gone awry:
That accursed Chynteñir
Looks ready to drive us hard.
Kakan’s people are a vast nation,
Their multitudes are like black worms in countless hosts.
Can any man stand equal to them?
Could one who matched them ever prosper?
Our strength will not suffice in battle.
Know that this is what I counsel;
Lion Kenen, heed my words.
Perhaps we should accept his demand,
Spare the people needless slaughter,
